Small-Sample Degrees of Freedom for Maximum Likelihood Intervals With Missing Data

Source: R/df_missing.R
df_missing.Rd

Computes the degrees of freedom of a t reference distribution for a Wald confidence interval from a full information maximum likelihood (FIML) fit, from each parameter's fraction of missing information (FMI), by either of von Hippel's (2016) two rules. The interval keeps the FIML estimate and its standard error and replaces the normal quantile with the t quantile on these degrees of freedom, which lengthens it by an amount that grows as the sample shrinks and as the share of the information lost to missing values grows.

Usage

df_missing(
  fmi,
  N = NULL,
  k = NULL,
  df_complete = NULL,
  method = c("effective_n", "complete_df"),
  floor = 3
)

Arguments

fmi

The fraction of missing information of each parameter: a numeric vector of values below 1, or the table returned by fraction_missing_information, whose fmi and N columns are used and whose term column labels the rows. The names of a named vector label the rows. A missing value gives missing degrees of freedom for that row.

N

The number of cases the fit used (with lavaan, the rows with at least one observed variable, lavInspect(fit, "nobs")), of length 1 or the length of fmi. Required by method = "effective_n" unless fmi is a table with an N column; not used by "complete_df".

k

The number of parameters subtracted from the effective sample size, of length 1 or the length of fmi: for a regression coefficient, the number of regression parameters (slopes and intercept), so that the complete data degrees of freedom are \(N - k\); for a factor loading or omega, 1, the value DMAR's calibration chose (see Details). Required by method = "effective_n", with no default.

df_complete

The complete data degrees of freedom, of length 1 or the length of fmi: the error degrees of freedom the interval would use if no value were missing (\(n - k\) for a regression coefficient, \(n - 1\) for a mean), not the model degrees of freedom of a structural equation model. Inf is allowed and gives the normal reference. Required by method = "complete_df", with no default.

method

"effective_n" (the default; von Hippel's Eq. 31, the rule his Table 5 used) or "complete_df" (his Eq. 32).

floor

The lower bound on the degrees of freedom: a single number of 0 or more. Defaults to 3, von Hippel's (2016) recommendation; 0 removes it.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with one row per value of fmi, in input order, and the columns term, df (the degrees of freedom, bounded below by floor), df_unbounded, fmi (the value used), N, k, df_complete, and at_floor (TRUE where the bound applied). A column the method does not use is NA: df_complete under "effective_n", k under "complete_df", and N under "complete_df" unless a table supplied it. The attributes method and floor record the call, and the printed table, at the console or knitted, is followed by a line naming the rule and the floor.

Details

Why a t reference distribution. A maximum likelihood Wald interval is the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times the standard error; the normal quantile comes from the large-sample distribution of the estimate. With incomplete data in small samples that interval is too short. In von Hippel's (2016) simulations of bivariate normal data with half the values of one variable missing, the normal FIML intervals at n = 25 covered 5 to 6 points below the nominal 95% for the intercept and slope of a regression and 8 to 14 points below it for the residual variance, and at n = 100 they were 0 to 3 points below (pp. 432–433). What fails is the reference distribution, not the estimate or its standard error: the normal quantile treats the standard error as known, and with few cases, or few effective cases once the missing information is subtracted, the standard error is itself estimated with error, as it is in a complete data regression whose coefficients are referred to t on \(N - k\) degrees of freedom. The t distribution is an approximation here, since the small-sample distribution of a FIML estimate is not exactly t (von Hippel, 2016, p. 431). Von Hippel's t intervals brought the coverage of most parameters to within 2 points of nominal (p. 434). At n = 25 it stayed below nominal for the parameters whose point estimates are biased, because a longer interval covers the variability of an estimate, not its bias.

The two rules. With \(\gamma\) the parameter's fraction of missing information, method = "effective_n" (von Hippel's \(\nu^*_{ML}\), his Eq. 31) is $$\nu^* = N(1 - \gamma) - k,$$ the complete data regression degrees of freedom \(N - k\) with \(N\) replaced by the effective sample size \(N(1 - \gamma)\), the number of complete cases that would carry the same information about the parameter (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012, p. 488). Here \(k\) is the number of regression parameters, slopes and intercept. With no missing information it is \(N - k\) exactly. method = "complete_df" (von Hippel's \(\nu_{ML}\), his Eq. 32) is $$\nu = \nu_{com} (1 - \gamma) \frac{\nu_{com} + 1}{\nu_{com} + 3},$$ where \(\nu_{com}\), given as df_complete, is the degrees of freedom the interval would use if no value were missing: the error degrees of freedom, not the model degrees of freedom of a structural equation model (p. 423). It is the limit of Barnard and Rubin's (1999) degrees of freedom for multiple imputation as the number of imputations grows, which von Hippel derives from the large-sample equivalence of maximum likelihood and multiple imputation with infinitely many imputations, and it is the observed data part of that formula (see df_barnard_rubin). With no missing information it gives \(\nu_{com}(\nu_{com} + 1)/(\nu_{com} + 3)\) rather than \(\nu_{com}\) (21.2 rather than 23 when \(\nu_{com}\) = 23); the factor comes from the observed data degrees of freedom and does not vanish with the missing information. The two rules agree closely: for a simple regression with n = 25, k = 2, and \(\gamma\) = .5 they give 10.6 and 10.5 (p. 432). Von Hippel's Table 5 used the effective sample size rule, and he reports very similar results with the general one (p. 433).

The floor. Either rule can return a small or negative value when the FMI is estimated near 1 or, for "effective_n", when the effective sample size approaches k. A t distribution with 2 or fewer degrees of freedom has no finite variance, and its quantiles grow without bound as the degrees of freedom approach 0 (a 95% interval on 1 degree of freedom uses 12.7), so von Hippel bounds the degrees of freedom below at 3 (his Eq. 34). floor = 3 is that bound. The unbounded value is kept in df_unbounded, and at_floor marks the rows where the bound applied. floor = 0 returns the unbounded "complete_df" value, which is never negative; a negative "effective_n" value becomes 0 there, which is not a usable reference distribution.

Where the FMI comes from. The FMI of a parameter is the share of its sampling variance due to the missing values, \(\gamma = 1 - SE_C^2 / SE_O^2\), with \(SE_C\) its standard error had the data been complete and \(SE_O\) its standard error from the incomplete data (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012, Eq. 4). It differs from parameter to parameter, and so do the degrees of freedom: a parameter estimated mostly from fully observed variables keeps nearly all of its degrees of freedom however many values are missing elsewhere. fraction_missing_information estimates it from a FIML fit, and its table can be passed as fmi directly; lavaan's parameterEstimates(fit, fmi = TRUE) gives another estimate. Some estimators return negative FMIs in small samples (Chen & Savalei, 2021); a negative FMI has no degrees of freedom interpretation, so a value below \(-10^{-8}\) is refused, and a value between that and 0, which is rounding error around a parameter with no missing information, is set to 0.

Which parameters the rules are supported for. Von Hippel's simulations used bivariate normal data with correlation .5, n = 25 and 100, and half the values of one variable missing, completely at random or whenever the other variable was negative (missing at random). The intervals evaluated were for the intercepts and slopes of the regression of each variable on the other, the mean of the incomplete variable, the covariance, and the variances (on a cube root scale). The rules therefore have published support for regression coefficients and for moments: means, variances, and covariances. They have none for factor loadings or for reliability coefficients such as omega, whose complete data intervals are themselves asymptotic, so that no complete data degrees of freedom are defined for them. For those, DMAR's own calibration study (in the package's source repository, methodology/missing_data; fa_confirmatory describes its design) simulated one factor models fit by FIML and found that method = "effective_n" with k = 1 brought the coverage of the loadings and of omega closer to .95 than the normal reference did: no cell's coverage, averaged over its loadings, exceeded .9502, and omega's .9550 (single loadings reached .9595 in the cells with missing values and .963 in the complete ones, where the rule is t on \(N - 1\) and the normal reference reached .962); it is the rule fa_confirmatory and reliability_omega apply under wald_df = "missing_information". For coefficient alpha no rule passed the study's decision rule, fixed before the run, which a coverage of .966 in one cell decided (see reliability_alpha).

These numerical results are conditional on the H1 eligibility rule the study applied. The affine-collapse diagnostic sets aside additional draws, and the study has not established coverage under that selection. A raw-data eligibility replay alone cannot validate the FMI refits and information diagnostics. The keyword is an approximate, opt-in rule, not a coverage guarantee.

The function has no default for k or df_complete, because the right value depends on the parameter.

References

Barnard, J., & Rubin, D. B. (1999). Small-sample degrees of freedom with multiple imputation. Biometrika, 86(4), 948–955. doi:10.1093/biomet/86.4.948

Chen, L., & Savalei, V. (2021). Three sample estimates of fraction of missing information from full information maximum likelihood. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 667802. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.667802

Savalei, V., & Rhemtulla, M. (2012). On obtaining estimates of the fraction of missing information from full information maximum likelihood. Structural Equation Modeling, 19(3), 477–494. doi:10.1080/10705511.2012.687669

von Hippel, P. T. (2016). New confidence intervals and bias comparisons show that maximum likelihood can beat multiple imputation in small samples. Structural Equation Modeling, 23(3), 422–437. doi:10.1080/10705511.2015.1047931

See also

df_barnard_rubin for the degrees of freedom of a multiple imputation estimate; mlmr for FIML regression.

Other missing data: cov_fiml(), df_barnard_rubin(), fraction_missing_information(), missing_coverage(), missing_patterns()

Examples

# von Hippel's (2016, p. 432) worked example: a simple regression with
# n = 25 cases, an intercept and a slope (k = 2), and half of the
# information about the slope missing.
df_missing(0.5, N = 25, k = 2)
#>  term        df     df_unbounded fmi   N  k df_complete at_floor
#>  parameter_1 10.500 10.500       0.500 25 2 <NA>        FALSE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule,
#> N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3
df_missing(0.5, df_complete = 23, method = "complete_df")
#>  term        df     df_unbounded fmi   N    k    df_complete at_floor
#>  parameter_1 10.615 10.615       0.500 <NA> <NA> 23          FALSE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 32) complete data rule,
#> df_complete (1 - fmi) (df_complete + 1) / (df_complete + 3), bounded below at 3

# Each parameter gets the degrees of freedom of its own FMI. With no
# missing information the effective sample size rule returns the
# complete data degrees of freedom, N - k = 23; near an FMI of 1 the
# floor of 3 takes over.
df_missing(c(slope = 0.5, intercept = 0.1, complete = 0, sparse = 0.95),
           N = 25, k = 2)
#>  term      df     df_unbounded fmi   N  k df_complete at_floor
#>  slope     10.500 10.500       0.500 25 2 <NA>        FALSE   
#>  intercept 20.500 20.500       0.100 25 2 <NA>        FALSE   
#>  complete  23     23           0.000 25 2 <NA>        FALSE   
#>  sparse    3      -0.750       0.950 25 2 <NA>         TRUE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule,
#> N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3

# A regression whose outcome is observed for only the 145 Grant-White
# students of 301: t26_flags is missing for every Pasteur student. mlmr()
# fits it by full information maximum likelihood (with the Wald interval,
# whose normal quantile the t reference replaces, and without the effect
# size refits, which this example does not use), and
# fraction_missing_information() gives each slope's FMI with the N behind
# it, so its rows go to df_missing() as they are; k = 3 counts the two
# slopes and the intercept.
fit <- mlmr(t26_flags ~ t1_visual_perception + t4_lozenges,
            data = holzinger_swineford, ci_method = "wald",
            effect_sizes = FALSE)
fmi <- fraction_missing_information(fit)
slopes <- fmi[fmi$op == "~", ]
dfs <- df_missing(slopes, k = 3)
dfs
#>  term                             df      df_unbounded fmi   N   k df_complete
#>  t26_flags ~ t1_visual_perception 136.521 136.521      0.536 301 3 <NA>       
#>  t26_flags ~ t4_lozenges          118.008 118.008      0.598 301 3 <NA>       
#>  at_floor
#>  FALSE   
#>  FALSE   
#> 
#> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule,
#> N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3

# The t interval keeps the FIML estimate and standard error and replaces
# the normal quantile. With more than a hundred effective cases the
# change is small; it matters when the effective sample size is small.
est <- coef(fit)[-1]
se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[-1]
crit <- qt(0.975, dfs$df)
data.frame(term = names(est), df = dfs$df,
           t_ci_lower = est - crit * se, t_ci_upper = est + crit * se,
           normal_ci_lower = est - qnorm(0.975) * se,
           normal_ci_upper = est + qnorm(0.975) * se, row.names = NULL)
#>                   term       df t_ci_lower t_ci_upper normal_ci_lower
#> 1 t1_visual_perception 136.5211  0.1988930  0.5693348       0.2005348
#> 2          t4_lozenges 118.0076  0.1735529  0.4819296       0.1751340
#>   normal_ci_upper
#> 1       0.5676930
#> 2       0.4803484
